A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same study, with matching authors, regret-loss formulation, and core experiments. All pages, including Appendices A-E, support comparison; relocated material and retained plots can be matched reliably.

before.justification: v3 reports original online-learning and repeated-game experiments, regret-loss training results, and empirical validation and ablations in the appendices.

after.justification: v4 retains those original results and adds correlation diagnostics, sequential-recommendation experiments, and simulated negotiation results in Appendix C.

M1.justification: The regret-loss objectives, Transformer parameterizations, optimization approach, and original full-information/bandit procedures are retained. Equations (5.1)-(5.3) are unchanged; moving architecture definitions into Section 2.2 does not introduce a new model.

E1.justification: Appendix C.10 adds sequential recommendation using real user-interaction data and uniformly random controls, plus natural-language negotiation between two LLMs. These substantially extend the retained synthetic loss-sequence and matrix-game coverage. The recommendation dataset is identified through Liu et al. (2023b), without a dataset name in the PDF.

E2.justification: OpenAI o1 joins GPT-4-Turbo in the new application comparisons. Existing FTRL, FTPL, Thompson Sampling, and UCB comparisons remain. The generalized-quantal-response comparator disappears from the noisy-alternating and adaptive-loss comparisons formerly displayed in Figure 4.1.

E3.justification: New protocols include equal-priority item-set recommendation with a miss-based regret metric, and negotiation evaluated through three alternative replies per turn, four LLM-scored criteria, and dynamic regret. Negotiation reports 10 scenarios per model and a 10-turn limit. Existing benchmark horizons, training budgets, and evaluation rules are retained.

E4.justification: Appendix C.2 adds temporal-correlation diagnostics for the trend test, and C.10.1 compares real recommendation histories with random controls. Conversely, Figure 4.1 removes both failure-regime checks of the quantal-response explanation. Existing prompt, history-summarization, and regret-loss parameter ablations remain.

E5.justification: Appendix C.2 newly makes the trend test's independence assumption explicit and discusses its binomial p-values as approximate under weak dependence. The calculation itself, existing repeated-experiment counts, and reporting of variability across environment instances remain unchanged.

E6.justification: New Figures C.9-C.10 report recommendation and negotiation outcomes; negotiation regression exponents are 0.67 for GPT-4-Turbo and 0.87 for o1. Figure C.1 adds correlation results. The two adverse-case quantal-response result panels are removed, while Tables 1-3 and the other retained plots preserve their results.

T1.justification: The principal theorems are retained. Appendix C.2 adds explicit independence assumptions and a moment-based argument for binomial approximation. Appendix E.7 also changes local algebra, including dropping the factor 2 from Equation (E.11); these edits do not constitute a new main guarantee.

C1.justification: The abstract and principal contributions retain the same claims: observed sublinear regret alongside failure cases, a hypothetical connection to FTPL, and an unsupervised regret-loss with generalization and optimization guarantees. Rewording and new application evidence do not redefine these core contributions.

C2.justification: v4 develops an in-context trend-prediction explanation and expands limitations concerning hypothetical theory, policy regret, and model scale. It removes the specific interpretation of quantal-response failures. Its new explanation of comparable or inferior LLM performance in games conflicts with retained Figure 5.3, which shows GPT-4 achieving lower regret.

D1.justification: Figure 3.5 newly specifies N = 1 for the regret-loss-trained models. Appendix C.10 documents negotiation construction, scoring, and a worked dialogue example, although recommendation setup details are largely delegated to a citation. Existing training hyperparameters in Appendix E.11 are unchanged.

R1.justification: v4 adds focused citations on recommendation, G-eval, multi-agent reinforcement learning, policy regret, and binomial approximation, and positions the application studies relative to that literature. Established comparisons with prior online-learning and in-context-learning research remain substantially intact.

P1.justification: v4 edits prose and headings, moves notation and Transformer definitions from Appendix B into Section 2, and relocates the illustrative training-data example to Appendix D.3. The overall narrative remains intact. A previously valid related-work cross-reference becomes an unresolved '??' in the introduction.

P2.justification: Three figures are added: correlation heatmaps and two application-result displays. Figure 4.1 becomes a wrapped single-panel figure after losing two panels. Other plots retain their graphics, with localized placement, caption, numbering, and typesetting changes.

improvement.justification: New application studies and explicit statistical assumptions improve coverage and transparency. However, v4 removes the quantal-response failure evidence and adds an interpretation inconsistent with Figure 5.3. The new studies' incompletely specified recommendation setup and LLM-based negotiation scoring limit their evidential strength, leaving the net quality direction unclear.
